title_original: À Paris, la fragilité des lieux de fête alternatifs qui ferment les uns après les autres
editorial_title_zh: 在巴黎，另类派对场所正一个接一个地陷入脆弱与消亡
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在巴黎，另类派对场所和文化第三方空间正一个接一个地关闭。在各种不同原因的背后，隐藏着同样的脆弱性：它们落脚于城市的缝隙中，却始终依赖于最终总会脱离其掌控的土地资产。

建立了一个低成本的第三方空间：艺术家驻留地、协会、派对、行为艺术表演……在五年时间里，这个场地就像是被暂存于城市一隅的世外桃源，一个距离环城公路仅数米之遥的创作与社交空间。就在去年6月30日，这段经历画上了句号：在免费提供场地多年后，业主选择在此建造一家酒店。这种现象并非孤例。与此同时，金箭剧场（La Flèche 曾主要接待酷儿群体、有色人种群体以及新兴艺术家。“我们失去的不仅仅是一个场地，而是一个完整的艺术生态系统、各种实践以及一座城市的创作活力，”伊德隆强调道。这些地方有一个共同点：它们通常落脚于城市尚未决定如何处置的地方。一座旧工厂、一个废弃的火车站、一块等待开发的土地……这些暂时避开市场压力的空间，孕育着传统经济难以资助的用途。“某种程度上，我们就是那些在建筑重回市场之前，装点空置场地的温顺木偶，”伊德隆总结道，“正是这一点，注定了它们的脆弱与短暂。”", En juin 2021, Arnaud Idelon et ses associés investissent une ancienne usine de Bagnolet. Dans ce bâtiment en sursis, Le Sample installe un tiers-lieu à bas coût : des résidences d’artistes, des associations, des fêtes, des performances… Pendant cinq ans, le site est un morceau de ville mis entre parenthèses, un espace de création et de sociabilité à quelques mètres du périphérique. Le 30 juin dernier, l’expérience s’est achevée : le propriétaire, après plusieurs années de mise à disposition à titre gracieux, a choisi d’y construire un hôtel. Le phénomène n’est pas isolé. Au même moment, La Flèche d’Or a cessé ses activités avant des travaux qui doivent permettre sa réouverture en 2027, tandis que son futur mode de gestion sera soumis à un appel à projets.

À l’automne, ce sera au tour de La Station – Gare des Mines de fermer pour près de trois ans, le temps du réaménagement de la porte d’Aubervilliers. Après dix ans de baux précaires, la Ville a prévu son implantation pérenne. Mais son modèle repose à 85 % sur ses recettes propres (billetterie, bar) : trois ans sans activité régulière, c’est un gouffre. Ces trajectoires ne racontent pas une seule crise. « Pas de cause unique, pas de responsable unique », nous prévient Idelon. Le Sample dépendait à seulement 6 % des subventions : sa fermeture relève d’abord d’un choix immobilier. À La Flèche d’Or, les travaux et la remise en jeu de la gestion rebattent les cartes. À La Station, c’est le calendrier de l’aménagement urbain. Fin 2025, Fawa, lieu de vie solidaire et queer installé sous le périphérique à porte de la Villette, a lui aussi été placé en liquidation judiciaire, après un lourd endettement lié à d’importants travaux de mise en sécurité.

Le provisoire, éternel talon d’Achille

Lorsque ces lieux disparaissent, ce ne sont pas seulement quelques soirées qui s’éteignent. Avec eux partent des espaces de travail pour les artistes, d’expérimentation ou de sociabilité pour des communautés qui disposent de peu d’options. La Flèche d’Or, Le Sample, La Station ou Fawa accueillaient notamment des communautés queer et racisées, ainsi que des artistes émergents. « On ne perd pas juste un lieu mais tout un écosystème artistique, des pratiques, le bouillonnement créatif d’une ville », insiste Idelon. Ces lieux ont un point commun : ils s’installent souvent là où la Ville n’a pas encore décidé quoi faire. Une ancienne usine, une gare désaffectée, un terrain en attente d’aménagement… Des espaces soustraits temporairement à la pression du marché, où s’inventent des usages que l’économie classique financerait difficilement. « D’une certaine manière, nous sommes les gentilles marionnettes qui animent des endroits vacants le temps que ces bâtiments reviennent dans le marché, résume Idelon. C’est ce qui les rend inévitablement précaires et temporaires. »

Pour Luca Pattaroni, sociologue et spécialiste de la contre-culture dans la ville gentrifiée, cette mécanique dépasse largement Paris. Les occupations temporaires offrent une chance aux acteurs culturels, mais les condamnent aussi à rester dans « un interstice », exposés à la concurrence de ce qui rapporte davantage. « L’objet culturel devient aussi un objet de jeu financier », observe-t-il. Même lorsqu’un lieu est propriété publique, comme La Flèche d’Or, il peut devenir une ressource foncière rare, soumise à des arbitrages, à une mise en concurrence, et au changement de couleur politique des municipalités. Ces fragilités se doublent d’un contexte national tendu, avec des baisses drastiques des financements publics de la culture depuis 2025. La disparition, en juin, du groupement d’intérêt public France Tiers-Lieux, qui coordonnait depuis 2022 la politique nationale en faveur des tiers-lieux, en est un autre signal. Le réseau dénonce un désengagement de l’État, tandis que celui-ci assure que les dispositifs seront poursuivis autrement.

D’après Pattaroni, cette évolution nourrit une contradiction : les pouvoirs publics encouragent les tiers-lieux et l’urbanisme transitoire, tout en demandant aux structures de se débrouiller par elles-mêmes. Les « anciens squatteurs sont parfois contraints de devenir des manageurs avec les marchés publics » . À mesure que les lieux sont institutionnalisés, ils gagnent parfois en reconnaissance ce qu’ils perdent en autonomie. « Soit on rentre dans les clous, soit on disparaît », résume-t-il. Alors, comment sortir de cette mécanique ? Idelon ne réclame pas simplement davantage de subventions. Le véritable levier serait foncier : créer des coopératives ou des sociétés civiles immobilières, recourir à des baux de longue durée, afin de sortir ces lieux de la seule logique du marché. Lorsque l’équipe du Sample envisageait de racheter le bâtiment qui les accueillait, une question revenait : « À partir de quand Le Sample n’est plus Le Sample ? » Augmenter les jauges, les prix ou les surfaces aurait permis une viabilité économique, mais au risque de détruire ce qui faisait précisément sa valeur. Pour Idelon, leur survie ne pourra donc pas reposer sur un seul acteur : propriétaires, artistes, société civile, collectivités et État doivent trouver ensemble des moyens de sécuriser ces espaces. Il ne s’agit donc pas seulement de trouver où danser demain, mais de savoir si la Ville veut encore préserver des lieux dont la valeur ne se mesure pas seulement à ce qu’ils rapportent.

article_text:
As the world mourns Sir Patrick Stewart ‘s death at age 86 , a longtime friend and collaborator is paying tribute to his legacy.

Sir Ian McKellen , who starred as Magneto opposite Stewart’s Professor X in the X-Men films, explained what made the late actor “a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love” after he Stewart’s rep revealed he died following a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

“Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end,” he began on Instagram . “You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.

‘Star Trek,’ ‘X-Men’ & ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Stars Remember Patrick Stewart: “A Singular Talent, A Generous Collaborator & A True Gentleman”

“We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in Star Trek . ‘But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marveled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes ( X-Men of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway.”

McKellen continued, “America was his adopted home, where he met his adored Sunny who has cared for him through sickness and health, through thick and thin. But he never forsook his origins: and the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as Chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire.

View this post on Instagram

“His farewell performance in Avengers: Doomsday is yet to be seen,” added McKellen after he and Stewart recently reprised their roles from the X-Men franchise in the upcoming MCU movie, which premieres Dec. 18 in theaters.

Stewart’s rep announced that the 3x Golden Globe-nominated actor died on Wednesday at his Los Angeles home, with wife Sunny Ozell by his side.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Lyrical Media and Embrace have sold feature package Butcher & Blackbird , a dark romance based on the bestselling novel by Brynne Weaver , to Amazon MGM Studios , for release worldwide on Prime Video.

Chris McKay , the filmmaker who directed Amazon’s Chris Pratt sci-fi actioner The Tomorrow War , is set to direct. Emma Laird ( War ) and Thomas Doherty ( Paradise ) will star.

Script is by Laura Kosann with revisions by Ari Berkowitz and Ava Tramer. Lyrical Media’s Alexander Black and Embrace will produce. Weaver and McKay will exec produce alongside Lyrical Media’s Arlen Konopaki, Jon Rosenberg, and Jonathan Faust.

The first installment of Ruinous Love , a #1 New York Times bestselling trilogy from Weaver, Butcher & Blackbird follows two competing killers who target other serial killers as they attempt to one up each other. As their unlikely bond grows into something deeper, they start to wonder if a future together could ever be possible.

Watch on Deadline

Published in October 2023, the book was a New York Times, USA Today, and Publisher’s Weekly bestseller that went viral on BookTok. Weaver’s books have been sold in over 25 countries with over five million copies sold to date.

English actress Laird is coming off of 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and the BBC series Mint , for which she was nominated for a BAFTA Scotland for Best Actress. Upcoming, she has Apple TV’s Neuromancer , Season 2 of HBO’s War , A24’s Elden Ring , The Housekeeper alongside Helena Bonham Carter, and Cary Joji Fukunaga’s Blood on Snow . She is repped by United Agents, manager Dara Gordon, CAA, and Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

Doherty is a Scottish actor who can currently be seen starring in Hulu’s Paradise . Past TV credits include Tell Me Lies , Gossip Girl , Girls5eva , High Fidelity and Catherine the Great . He is repped by Anonymous Content, Gersh, and Peikoff Mahan.

McKay is also known for his work on the Lego film series, including as director of The Lego Batman Movie , and for the Uni vampire comedy Renfield starring Nicolas Cage and Nicholas Hoult. He is repped by UTA, Rise Management, and Yorn Levine.

Currently adapting Ali Hazelwood’s novel Deep End for Netflix with 21 Laps and Unwell producing, Kosann is repped by CAA, Untitled, and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern.

Lyrical Media’s upcoming film slate includes Osgood Perkins’ The Young People for Neon and The Troop with Paramount Primal. Their animation arm is producing Bloodborne alongside PlayStation Productions and creator Seán McLoughlin (aka JackSepticEye), with Lyrical Media co-financing alongside Sony Pictures. Additionally, Lyrical Animation will produce a feature adaptation of Godslap , the comic created by YouTuber and streamer Charlie “MoistCr1TiKaL” White.

Credits for Embrace (formerly Ryder Picture Company) include Dumb Money , Bruiser , I Love Boosters , the Netflix romantic comedy Office Romance , and A24 releases The Death of Robin Hood and Onslaught . They’re currently in post on Shiver starring Keanu Reeves for Warner Bros. and Mother’s Helper , starring Shailene Woodley.

Berkowitz and Tramer are repped by Artists First and Ginsburg Daniels Kallis. Berkowitz is also repped by CAA.

Book）和《波西米亚狂想曲》（Bohemian Rhapsody）统治颁奖季的那一年，它堪称最令人尴尬的奥斯卡得主。相比之下，当他把迄今为止最具个人色彩的作品《解放》（The Liberation）核心所依托的真实故事搬上银幕时，其框架的处理方式或许还算更有品味一些。影片灵感源于他祖母在20世纪80年代初被洗脑加入邪教的经历，纳提夫不断试图在其青年时期的集中营经历与被招募进入一个要求她疏远家庭、医疗以及任何来自外部世界不受欢迎干扰的组织之间，建立起生硬的类比。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "丽塔·库珀（凯莉·库恩饰）被年轻的邪教领袖里基·金（莉莉·詹姆斯饰）洗脑的时间本身就令人心碎，但当它被构筑为她作为大屠杀幸存者创伤的延续时，这种经历就显得极其微不足道了。《解放》将某些针对人类的最严重罪行进行了一定程度的琐碎化，因为它将全女性邪教隐蔽的“哈莫尼娅”公社背景化，恋恋不舍地聚焦于将邪教罪行与外部世界隔离开来的篱笆，并引入其成员身着几乎相同的服装进行无偿体力劳动。如果这种视觉上的平行还不够清晰，丽塔的小女儿埃拉（贝拉·拉姆齐饰）则强调，她疏离的妈妈看起来“就像刚从集中营里出来一样”。丽塔童年的背景对于确立她为何会被一个坚称能帮她摆脱一生所背负恐怖的邪教领袖所胁迫至关重要，但这段难以想象的恐怖过去被引用得如此笨拙，以至于变得令人反感。", "这些是纳提夫和诺阿·伯曼-赫兹伯格剧本中的缺陷，而并非库恩一如既往的出色表演的问题。影片通过两条独立的故事情节展开——1982年，抑郁的办公室职员丽塔首次遇到里基；以及1984年，埃拉和她的大女儿乔（敖德萨·杨饰）追踪到邪教的新公社——这位女演员有效地表达了未处理的情绪如何会将她带入邪教温暖的怀抱，以及一旦落入其网罗，她为什么会如此抗拒任何去洗脑的呼吁。她在这样一个高要求角色中的游刃有余，很可能是因为我们曾在《守望尘世》的三季中看过她处理过这一悲伤回避故事情节的更具挑战性的变体，在这部剧中，每一个超现实的迂回都是她在失去家人后试图重获某种秩序感的结果。相比之下，在《解放》中更容易从情感上把握这些素材，因此默认情况下要求更低。她让她的过去与现在之间的关系显得比剧本所暗示的、那种整齐划一的过去创伤延续更加凌乱、更有血有肉。它是基于真实的恐怖，但呈现出来的效果却像是一部打磨过度的《玛莎·玛丽·麦茜·玛露》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《解放》在1984年的段落中最为奏效——尽管在1982年的序列中，饰演库恩丈夫的、令人愉快的脾气暴躁的特雷西·莱茨缺席令人遗憾——此时小女儿试图拯救母亲，而大女儿则被里基的生活方式所催眠。它越来越像是一部关于高墙逼近这个家庭的惊悚片，尤其是当埃拉意识到如果她的糖尿病姐姐任由其自生自灭，反医疗政策将会带来多么灾难性的后果时，拉姆齐作为这一段落的情感中心，奉献了她最佳的银幕表现之一。", article_text:
Nobody makes clumsier social allegories than Guy Nattiv. His first American effort, the 2018 short Skin , followed a violent white supremacist who was kidnapped, drugged, and held hostage while his entire skin was tattooed jet-black as revenge for a hate crime; it was the most-embarrassing Oscar winner in a year when Green Book and Bohemian Rhapsody dominated the ceremony. That is arguably more tasteful than how he frames the true story at the heart of his most personal effort to date, The Liberation . Inspired by his grandmother’s indoctrination into a cult in the early 1980s, Nattiv keeps attempting to draw heavy-handed parallels between her youth in a concentration camp and recruitment into an organization that asked her to shun family, healthcare, and any other unwelcome intrusions from the outside world.

Rita Cooper’s (Carrie Coon) time being brainwashed by younger cult leader Ricki King (Lily James) is harrowing on its own, but looks deeply insignificant when framed as a continuation of her trauma as a Holocaust survivor. The Liberation trivializes some of the gravest crimes against humanity for how it frames the all-female cult’s secluded Harmonia commune, lingering on the fences that separate its crimes from the outside world and introducing its members doing unpaid manual labor in near-matching outfits. If such visual parallels weren’t clear enough, Rita’s youngest daughter Ella (Bella Ramsey) stresses that her distant mom looks like “she’s just got out of the camps.” The context of Rita’s childhood is important in establishing why she’d be coerced by a group leader adamant she can rid her of the horrors she’s carried her entire life, but that unimaginably horrifying past is invoked so clumsily it becomes distasteful.

These are flaws with Nativ and Noa Berman-Herzberg’s screenplay, not Coon’s characteristically terrific performance. Told across two separate storylines––in 1982, when the depressed office drone Rita first meets Ricki, and 1984, when Ella and her older daughter Jo (Odessa Young) track down the cult’s new commune––the actress effectively articulates how unprocessed emotions could lead her into a cult’s warm embrace, and why she would be so reluctant to any calls to deprogram once caught in its web. Her ease in such a demanding role is likely because we saw her tackle a more challenging variant on this grief-avoidance storyline during three seasons of The Leftovers , where each surreal detour was a result of trying to regain some sense of order after losing her family. The Liberation , where it’s much easier to get an emotional handle on this material, is less demanding by default. She makes the relationship between her past and present seem messier, more human than the neatly drawn continuation of past trauma the screenplay suggests. It’s based on true horrors, but comes across like a too-polished Martha Marcy May Marlene .

The Liberation is most effective in its 1984 stretches––although the absence of a delightfully crotchety Tracy Letts, stunt cast as Coon’s husband in the 1982 sequences, is felt––as the younger daughter tries saving her mother while the older becomes hypnotized by Ricki’s way of life. It increasingly resembles a thriller about walls closing in on the family, especially when Ella realizes how disastrous the anti-healthcare policy could be if her diabetic sister is left to fend for herself, and Ramsey has one of her best theatrical showcases as the emotional center of this stretch.

In fact, the only weak link of this ensemble is James as the cult leader; she fails to convince as an emotionally manipulative figure who could bring women her senior under her spell. The brief suggestion that it’s because she awakens suppressed sapphic desires is more tangible, though the screenplay discards that idea almost as soon as it’s introduced. James is a particularly strange casting decision considering she replaced Vicky Krieps, whose offbeat energy can have an undercurrent of menace if applied correctly. It’s admirable that James wanted to be cast against type so boldly, but she doesn’t have the built-in intensity required to make me suspend disbelief that she could manipulate her way under someone’s skin. Through her leadership, it becomes a cult of no personality.

The Liberation is Nattiv’s strongest effort to date, but that’s not saying much, and it’s thanks entirely to an almost uniformly excellent ensemble elevating his material. He remains as clumsy as ever in transforming his stories into incisive social commentary.

The Liberation screened at the BFI London Film Festival and opens on January 8, 2027.

Una delle novità proposte durante la Torino Art Week è il progetto Fonogrammi , una nuova serie di commissioni sonore ideate da artisti, musicisti, storici dell’arte e scrittori, invitati a interpretare la Collezione Cerruti attraverso inediti percorsi audio. Gli interventi scardinano la forma della tradizionale visita guidata, diventando teatro di performance sonore, tra composizioni musicali e narrazioni ispirate al percorso della Collezione.

Inoltre, in occasione della grande mostra dedicata a Marisa Merz in tre sedi, Castello di Rivoli, Fondazione Merz e GAM, con INTERFERENZE #7: MARISA MERZ , in programma fino al 4 aprile 2027, due opere dell’artista torinese sono state inserite nella Collezione per l’Art Week. Il programma, che mette in relazione la Collezione con l’arte contemporanea, vedrà nel percorso una scultura (Senza titolo, n.d.) che dialoga con quelle di Alberto Giacometti , Arturo Martini e Medardo Rosso , e un’opera su carta (Senza titolo, 2010-2012), collocata accanto ad un dipinto di Francis Bacon , creando nuovi accostamenti.

Fino al 28 febbraio 2027 è in mostra anche il secondo capitolo di Palinsesti , a cura di Luca Cena per riscoprire il nucleo librario della Collezione. Con PALINSESTI #2: PERFECT BINDING , le rare edizioni pregiate sono state prelevate dagli scaffali della biblioteca e distribuite tra le stanze della Villa. I volumi, con copertine rilegate a mano e databili dal Quattrocento al Novecento, rappresentano una parte importante dell’eredità di Cerruti.

Infine, con UNICUM , è stata posta l’attenzione su un particolare oggetto, isolato dal contesto originario e messo in mostra in un percorso insieme ad altre opere e oggetti legati allo stesso tema. Il progetto è guidato da specialisti e, per questa prima edizione, UNICUM #1, Beatrice Campi, storica dell’arte ed esperta di arte islamica e indiana, ha proposto un approfondimento su un tappeto safavide in seta.

A proposito di Fonogrammi, per la prima edizione sono stati invitati Beatrice Bonino x Any, Jeremy Deller, Giorgio Di Domenico e Siôn Parkinson. Gli autori hanno realizzato quattro audioguide, scaricabili dal sito della Fondazione e ascoltabili in Villa Cerruti e altrove. Durante questa Art Week, le loro performance sonore sono state presentate dal vivo a Cripta747, con THE PHONOGRAMS VARIETY SHOW .

Trasportando l’universo di Cerruti all’interno del centro culturale indipendente che dal 2008 sostiene la ricerca e la produzione artistica contemporanea, gli artisti hanno così esaudito il desiderio di Francesco Federico Cerruti di rendere accessibile la sua preziosa Collezione. La serata si è articolata in quattro atti, aprendosi con Any Lamentation (The Lowest Level of the Human Mood) , la composizione elettroacustica per arpa, realizzata da Any, nome d’arte della musicista Anastasia Patellis, in dialogo con l’artista Beatrice Bonino. La performance ha esplorato e tradotto in suono l’universo di Cerruti, restituendo il desiderio, la soddisfazione e l’inquietudine che si celavano dietro ognuno dei suoi acquisti.

Le note dell’arpa hanno avvolto gli ascoltatori in un paesaggio ambient rarefatto, costruito attraverso brevi sequenze sonore che si ripetevano ciclicamente, sovrapponendosi e stratificandosi lentamente. Il desiderio ha così assunto la forma di una tensione costante, simile a un lamento sospeso, che sembrava non trovare mai una piena risoluzione.

Lo spettacolo è proseguito con Desired Objects: Desire and Desires in the Cerruti Collection , la narrazione di Giorgio Di Domenico, che ha proposto una lettura storica dell’universo di Francesco Federico Cerruti e delle opere della sua Collezione. Il racconto ha attraversato le diverse sfumature del desiderio: dalla passione che anima l’atto del collezionare fino all’ossessione del possesso, passando per il bisogno di essere ricordati e amati. È emersa anche l’idea della Collezione come una relazione profonda e totalizzante, dalla quale risulta difficile separarsi. Le aspirazioni del collezionista si sono così intrecciate con quelle degli artisti, attraverso una rilettura delle opere acquisite da Cerruti, indagate nei loro significati e nelle loro possibili interpretazioni.

È seguito Antechamber: A Musical di Siôn Parkinson, una performance sonora in cui il suono della cornamusa scozzese di Robbie Donald è diventato la base per un intreccio di canto e sonorità noise di Parkinson. Ne è nato un momento sospeso, uno spazio simile a un’anticamera. La Villa è stata così trasportata fino a Cripta747, trasformata in una partitura, mentre la voce di Parkinson riecheggiava tra le sue pareti.

A chiudere la serata è stato Jeremy Deller con una lettura accompagnata da un video e da un accompagnamento sonoro di sottofondo che, attingendo a materiali d’archivio e alla storia della Villa e di Cerruti, ha dato voce alla collezione. Un viaggio dalla costa orientale dell’Inghilterra fino alla biblioteca della Villa. Il punto di partenza della narrazione è un villaggio del Norfolk, individuato da Deller nell’atlante seicentesco di John e William Blaeu, il Grande Atlante del 1662, conservato nella Collezione e luogo che l’artista frequenta abitualmente. Proprio da lì Deller ha registrato parte del racconto, riportando alla luce la storia del villaggio, segnato da un incendio che ha rischiato di coinvolgere una centrale nucleare.

Con la maestria di un documentarista, Deller intreccia frammenti di storia e ricordi personali, costruendo una nuova composizione: un racconto che sembra voler dare continuità e cura alla storia di Cerruti.

Ed è proprio questo lo spirito che anima i progetti della Fondazione Cerruti, nata per conservare e valorizzare la sua collezione, nel rispetto delle volontà testamentarie del suo fondatore, Francesco Federico Cerruti . La Fondazione Cerruti porta avanti un percorso di apertura e rilancio, volto a rendere sempre più accessibile al pubblico la sua Collezione, custodita nella Villa sulle colline di Rivoli. Una raccolta eclettica che attraversa secoli di storia dell’arte, dal Medioevo alla contemporaneità, e che si apre sempre più a nuove occasioni di dialogo con il presente. Nato a Genova e proveniente da una famiglia di ceto medio, Francesco Federico Cerruti aveva appreso dal padre e dall’attività di famiglia, dedicata alla legatoria industriale, il valore della diligenza e del lavoro. Da qui ha avuto inizio il suo percorso di collezionista, uno dei più raffinati del suo tempo, guidato da un gusto personale e ben definito. Oggi Villa Cerruti contiene libri, opere d’arte e arredi disposti così come lui stesso li aveva immaginati, restituendo al pubblico non soltanto una collezione, ma anche il mondo e la visione di chi l’ha creata.

article_text:
Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin know a thing or two about extreme athletes. From the daring rock climbing of “Free Solo” to their new film “Everest: The Other Side,” which follows Jim Morrison’s attempts to fulfill his late wife Hilaree Nelson’s dream of skiing down the world’s tallest mountain, the documentarians love to capture fearless people drawn to extreme challenges.

During a conversation about “Everest” with IndieWire features writer Alison Foreman at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, the filmmakers discussed what draws them to the subject matter over and over again.

“In all our films, you think you’re seeing these exceptional, extraordinary, extreme athletes. But at the end of the day they’re still human beings like the rest of us,” Chin said. “What I’m interested in bridging that gap where people feel like they can’t relate to people out there doing these things. But the story is really human, and this film is about very human experiences. Even though they’re climbing and skiiing the most extreme places in the world.”

Vasarhelyi also emphasized the fact that each documentary subject is a different person with their own unique story to tell. In the case of Nelson, she saw someone who was deeply goal-oriented but lacked the grand romanticizations about her sport that drive so many other athletes. She saw the adventurer as a fellow parent who lived a fairly normal life when she wasn’t pushing herself to scale the world’s highest peaks.

“I had met a lot of extreme athletes, but Hilaree had a candor to her vocation that I hadn’t heard before,” Vasarhelyi said. “It’s not romantic. She says in the film, ‘I know it’s just a mountain, but it’s everything to me. And I’m like a dog with a bone.’ And I understand that.”

National Geographic will release “Everest: The Other Side” in theaters on Friday, October 30. Watch the complete conversation in the video above.

Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com , or find us on Facebook , Twitter , Instagram , and YouTube .

Non sono mancati i record: Eva Helene Pade (£167,700) e Joseph Yaeger (£645.000, partendo da £120.000–180.000) hanno entrambi polverizzato le stime, stabilendo nuovi primati mondiali all’incanto.

«Finora è stata una settimana straordinaria per Londra: l’energia di Frieze ha dato un notevole impulso al mercato», ha dichiarato Olivia Thornton , Deputy Chairwoman, Modern & Contemporary Art, Europe di Phillips. «La vendita è iniziata con risultati di grande rilievo: le prime due opere in catalogo, firmate da Eva Helene Pade e Joseph Yaeger, hanno superato nettamente le rispettive stime massime, stabilendo nuovi record mondiali d’asta per entrambi gli artisti. Il risultato più importante della serata è stato raggiunto da Mathis di Gerhard Richter, proveniente dalla collezione di Marcel Brient. Anche Keep Ou T di Banksy, alla sua prima apparizione in asta, ha ottenuto un risultato significativo, raggiungendo 1,6 milioni di sterline».

Thornton ha inoltre evidenziato come questi risultati confermino «il costante interesse dei collezionisti per opere di qualità e di provenienza prestigiosa». Un’indicazione che aiuta a leggere il significato della vendita al di là delle cifre: in un contesto internazionale competitivo, la selezione delle opere e la loro storia collezionistica continuano a essere elementi decisivi per intercettare la domanda. Accanto alle aggiudicazioni pubbliche, Phillips ha curato l’intermediazione dell’acquisizione privata di 22 opere provenienti dalla collezione di Dartington Hall, con il sostegno dell’Art Fund. La casa d’aste ha inoltre presentato a Londra una spledida Tête di Amedeo Modigliani, in vista della vendita serale di New York prevista per il mese successivo, confermando una programmazione strategica che mette in relazione le principali piazze del mercato. Lo vedi a Londra, lo compri a New York. Il famoso «sistema».

Non finisce ovviamente qui. Gli appuntamenti di Phillips proseguono con l’asta Modern & Contemporary Art di sabato e con la vendita Modern & Contemporary Art and Design in programma la settimana prossima a Parigi, nel calderone di Art Basel e della Paris Art Week. Intanto, il risultato londinese consegna a Phillips un bilancio decisamente positivo e si aggiunge alle performance delle altre grandi case d’asta, componendo il quadro di una settimana particolarmente significativa per il mercato dell’arte.

article_text:
Canada , an esteemed New York gallery, faced the threat of closure last year after a backer filed two lawsuits against the space’s founders.

A New York court ruled that the gallery could remain open, and neither lawsuit appears to be active, with the most recent filings for both posted at the start of this year.

However, in the year and a half since the lawsuits were filed, three of Canada’s partners—including one of the gallery’s founders—left the operation. Five artists have also exited the gallery, among them Joan Snyder, who was added to Luhring Augustine’s roster last week.

Jean Lignel, a French collector, filed his lawsuits in February 2025 with the New York County Supreme Court. One of his lawsuits sought the dissolution of Canada, while the other alleged that the gallery’s other partners had improperly withdrawn more than $3 million, something that they denied in a counterclaim against Lignel.

The Canada partners’ counterclaim was discontinued earlier this year. Though Lignel’s lawsuits have gone through a series of appeals, neither seems to be currently ongoing.

Lignel began conversations with the gallery in 2008 as a recession wrought havoc upon the New York art market and the global economy. A 2008 document submitted alongside the lawsuit shows that Canada founders Sarah Braman, Suzanne Butler, Phil Grauer, and Wallace Whitney agreed to bring on Lignel as a backer. According to the agreement, Lignel paid $150,000 in exchange for a 50 percent ownership stake in the gallery.

In one of his lawsuits, Lignel alleged that, between 2009 and 2023, Canada’s founders “withdrew” more than $3 million, which he claimed ran “in violation of the operating agreement.” In their counterclaim, the Canada founders said that Lignel “knew that the Founding Members were being compensated for the services,” and that the “compensation for their services is well below market—the going rate for partner salaries for New York art galleries comparable to the Gallery is between $350,000 to $395,000 per year.”

In May 2025, a judge quickly denied the motion to dissolve Canada, saying that Lignel had failed to prove that the gallery couldn’t operate according to the terms of the agreement he signed. Moreover, the judge said, Lignel “concedes that the gallery has recently hired additional managers, who are not LLC members, thereby demonstrating that the gallery is a functioning business.”

“CANADA’s four founding members—Phil Grauer, Sarah Braman, Wallace Whitney and Suzy Butler—were deeply disappointed that Mr. Lignel, their Paris-based business partner, did not support the Gallery as it expanded its operations, including during a challenging period in the art market, and subsequently sought its dissolution through litigation,” a lawyer for the Canada partners told ARTnews in an email. “However, as the Court’s decision confirmed, the Gallery remains fully operational and continues its artist-run, community-focused programming and mission. While CANADA regrets that the members’ dispute involved court intervention, the Gallery remains hopeful that it can work collaboratively with Mr. Lignel in the future.”

A lawyer for Lignel did not respond to ARTnews ’s request for comment. ARTnews has also reached out to a Canada spokesperson for comment on Lignel’s involvement in the gallery and the departures of the three partners and five artists since his suits were filed.

According to a 6sqft profile of Lignel from 2016, the year he put his West Village home on the market for $14.5 million, he is a music producer, publisher, and entrepreneur with a collection that includes works by Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Ida Applebroog, and more. His involvement with Canada had not been reported prior to the lawsuits, which have gone unmentioned in the press until now.

Canada, whose roster includes artists such as Joe Bradley, Katherine Bernhardt, Katherine Bradford, Samara Golden, and Rachel Eulena Williams, first opened in 1999. It continues to operate a gallery in Tribeca, at 60 Lispenard Street, to which it moved in 2019 . Exhibitions by Scott and Tyson Reeder closed there this past weekend.

For a period, the gallery also operated an annex space across the street. But in August 2025, after Lignel’s lawsuits were filed, Canada subleased the annex gallery to dealer Max Levai, who has since moved his gallery to Chelsea. “We couldn’t afford to keep both of the spaces,” Wallace Whitney, a Canada founder, told Artnet News at the time. “And now, like many galleries, we are buckling down for a long haul. We want to stick around as long as possible.”

Partners and Artists Depart

While Lignel’s lawsuits were pending, Canada appears to have quietly scaled down its operations behind the scenes.

A comparison of Canada’s current staff page on its website and a version from October 2025 that was saved by the Internet Archive suggests that the gallery has shed two partners in the past year. Suzanne Butler, a Canada founder who was a defendant in Lignel’s lawsuits, is no longer listed as a partner. Tif Sigfrids, who closed her gallery in Athens, Georgia , in 2024 and joined Canada as a partner, also quietly left the gallery. Sigfrids declined to comment; ARTnews was unable to reach Butler.

One more partner left ahead of Butler and Sigfrids: Christiana Ine-Kimba Boyle, who exited her post as senior director of Pace Gallery in 2024 to become a partner and co-owner of Canada, where she formerly worked as a senior director. In March 2025, after only two and a half months as partner and co-owner at Canada, Boyle launched her own itinerant gallery, Gladwell Projects, which has staged exhibitions in Harlem, Jersey City, and Paris. She declined to comment.

An archived version of Canada’s roster available via the Wayback Machine also suggests that the gallery has shed five artists since Lignel’s lawsuits were filed: Matt Connors, Jess Fuller, Daniel Hesidence, Robert Janitz, and Joan Snyder. (The gallery has also added one artist, Kahlil Robert Irving , who gained representation with Canada last December.)

Snyder, who is now represented by both Luhring Augustine and Thaddaeus Ropac, said in an email to ARTnews that she had been previously unaware of the lawsuits and that she left Canada “under amicable circumstances.” She also noted that her two shows at the gallery had been “successful.”

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: HBO has set a November 17 premiere date for When a Witness Recants , director Dawn Porter ’s searing film about the toll of the longest combined wrongful conviction case in U.S. history.

The documentary executive produced by award-winning author Ta-Nehisi Coates will also be available to stream on HBO Max. It examines a gross miscarriage of justice that saw three teenage boys in Baltimore convicted of a murder they didn’t commit and sent to prison for life. Lauren Lipscomb, chief of the Baltimore State’s Attorney’s Conviction Integrity Division, who helped win freedom for the three after they spent 36 years in prison, calls it “the most egregious wrongful conviction case in my career.”

When a Witness Recants premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January and won the Audience Award at the recent Mill Valley Film Festival in Northern California. Watch the trailer below.

Watch on Deadline

“In 1983, a 14-year-old boy was murdered in the hallway of Harlem Park Junior High School in Baltimore, Maryland,” states a synopsis. “Three local teenagers were swiftly arrested, convicted, and sentenced to life in maximum security prisons. The truth is that they were all innocent. When a Witness Recants explores the collateral damage the handling of the case had on the close-knit community, the decades-long aftereffects on the wrongfully accused, and on the witnesses who decades later recanted their testimony and explained that they had been pressured as teenagers to give false testimony at trial, betraying the three accused.”

The synopsis continues, “Rediscovering the story as an adult, acclaimed author Ta-Nehisi Coates, who grew up in the same West Baltimore community, learns the truth about the case and comes to see it as both a crucial turning point for Baltimore’s tight knit Black community and a glaring example of a broader national crisis of racially charged police misconduct. Using animated sequences, insight from the major players, and footage from depositions taken in 2022, the film details how coerced confessions and false testimony led to the convictions, revealing an egregious abuse of authority and prosecutorial malfeasance.”

When a Witness Recants is adapted from a New Yorker article by Jennifer Gonnerman. The film includes a riveting scene where the exonerated men — Ransom Watkins, Andrew Stewart, and Alfred Chestnut – meet face-to-face with a man who recanted his testimony that had helped convict the trio decades earlier. “With raw emotion,” the synopsis notes, “the four men, now in their 50s and all survivors of a flawed criminal justice system, tell their stories as they seek to rebuild their lives in the wake of lost time.”

HBO Documentary Films presents When a Witness Recants , a Maceo-Lyn Production in association with Trilogy Films and Sony Pictures Television-Nonfiction. The film is directed by Dawn Porter and produced by Porter, Jennifer Oko, and Miriam Weintraub. Executive producers are Ta-Nehisi Coates, Kenyatta Matthews, Kamilah Forbes, Eli Holzman, Aaron Saidman, and Jennifer Gonnerman. For HBO, executive producers are Nancy Abraham, Lisa Heller, and Sara Rodriguez.

“The documentary puts a period on a part of my life I would like to forget, but it gives me a platform to maybe help other people as well,” Andrew Stewart said during a Q&A after a screening of the film at DC/DOX in June. “This documentary, I want this to highlight the better part of my life — coming home at 53, finding the love of my life and being happy.”

“Every time we look at [the film], it’s a reminder and it’s emotional for all three of us,” Alfred Chestnut said. “I don’t take nothing for granted — all my blessings. You see my daughter on the film, and I got another one on the way. I’m just looking forward to all the things that’s coming that God has for all three of us.”

Porter’s directing credits include Luther: Never Too Much (2024), The Lady Bird Diaries (2023), Rise Again: Tulsa and the Red Summer (2021), and J ohn Lewis: Good Trouble (2020). She also served as an EP on HBO’s Eyes on the Prize III: We Who Believe in Freedom Cannot Rest .

At the DC/DOX Q&A, she said, “It’s hard to understand how people who are innocent get convicted. And I’m very sad to say I have seen this too many times and it never stops shocking me and enraging me… We should not be a society that wrongfully puts children in prison for the rest of their lives ever, but certainly not for something they didn’t do.”

article_text:
Ever since 4DX technology debuted in 2009 for Seoul screenings of James Cameron’s “Avatar,” the immersive format has been associated primarily with spectacles and franchise films; if you’ve been to a 4DX auditorium, you probably went to see a Marvel movie or a “ Fast and Furious ” sequel. The idea seems to be that 4DX — a presentation system that “enhances” movies with physical effects like shaking seats, wind, flashing lights, snow, water, and scents — is best utilized in action films where the onscreen chaos is intensified by the chaos of being yanked around in your chair while nozzles spray air and water in your face.

For years, I avoided 4DX like the plague after an ill-advised trip to see “Maleficent: Mistress of Evil.” When motion sickness set in before the end of the first reel, I figured I had experienced enough 4DX to last me for the rest of my life. Then last year, while writing a piece comparing six release formats for “ One Battle After Another ,” I gave 4DX another shot and was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. Seeing Paul Thomas Anderson’s masterpiece with effects that included air blasting in my ear to simulate gunshots and the seat rocking to simulate Sean Penn’s masturbation added an unexpected dimension to the viewing experience.

Since then, I’ve caught a couple more movies in 4DX, from an epic that typically uses the format (“The Odyssey”) to a contained thriller that barely uses it at all (“Verity”). Then, last night, I caught the “Citizen Kane” of 4DX movies, the one that uses the format the way it should have always been implemented — not as a form of cinematic shock treatment designed to amplify onscreen violence, but as an expression of sensual pleasure. I give you, ladies and gentlemen, “ Wicker ” in 4DX.

Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson’s offbeat love story between a fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) and a man made of wicker (Alexander Skarsgård) has been a hot topic among cinephiles since its audience-pleasing debut at Sundance earlier this year. Hilarious but also genuinely romantic and poignant, it’s a true original. It’s also, as viewers could tell even from the trailer, fearlessly sexy, with several scenes of woman-on-wicker lovemaking that end with Colman’s bed demolished.

As soon as audiences started discovering the movie, the joke began making its way around Film Twitter and Letterboxd: where was the 4DX version of “Wicker?” Distributor Black Bear heard the joke and decided to make it a reality, scheduling one-night-only 4DX screenings at around 60 U.S. screens last night. If Southern California is any indication, the screenings were a wild success; the one I attended at a local Regal was nearly sold out, as were all the engagements within a 30-mile radius of Los Angeles.

And the 4DX presentation of “Wicker” did not disappoint. While many of the effects were typical of 4DX — the seat moving in unison with different characters, water hitting your face in rainy scenes — it didn’t take long for “Wicker” to demonstrate that it would be a more inventive, more adult exploitation of the format. The first sign of the picture’s flair for 4DX innovation came when Colman peed into her chamber pot and then tossed the contents out the door — and into the audience’s face, as we were all doused with water representing Colman’s urine.

Similarly cheeky gags occurred throughout the presentation, but the moment we were all waiting for was Colman and Skarsgård’s wedding night. The scene did not disappoint; as the fisherwoman and her wicker husband threw each other around the bed in ecstasy, the 4DX chairs tossed the audience in perfectly timed thrusts, creating a communal experience unlike any I’ve ever had in a movie theater. To be blunt, it felt like 150 strangers were all simulating sex with each other, and the, for lack of a better word, release at the end was exhilarating. We all erupted with applause when the bed split apart, and our shared ecstasy had reached its climax.

It makes one wonder: Is the true future of 4DX softcore pornography? There’s nothing really special about being jerked side to side while Superman flies through Metropolis, but feeling like you’re humping Olivia Colman (or being humped by Alexander Skarsgård) really brings people together. The possibilities for expanding the format’s potential are endless. Just as movies like “Titanic” and “Terminator 2” are retrofitted with 3D for special re-releases, 4DX could bring back “9 1/2 Weeks” and “Basic Instinct” in all their steamy, thrusting glory.

The fact that this was only a one-night event made it feel undeniably special, but today Black Bear announced that additional 4DX screenings are now scheduled throughout the next week. I’m glad the experiment was a success and has inspired an extension — the pleasures of “Wicker” in 4DX should not be limited to a select few.

article_text:
Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi has received a five-year-and-one-month prison sentence in absentia from Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court.

The Oscar-nominated director returned to his home country earlier this year after a global awards push for his thriller “It Was Just an Accident,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes Film Festival in May 2025 ahead of a dedicated Academy Awards campaign. Panahi has previously been arrested and imprisoned numerous times by Iranian authorities, and was once placed on house arrest and banned from filmmaking activities.

IndieWire learned of the sentencing from a release by Mansour Jahani, an independent film journalist based in Tehran who has regularly covered the legal repercussions Panahi has faced. According to the report, Panahi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said Panahi was also issued a two-year travel ban and a two-year prohibition on social media activity.

Nili also stated that Panahi’s bank accounts were frozen last week. This prompted a meeting with the Enforced of Judgments Unit at Iran ‘s Cultural and Media Prosecutor’s Office, which revealed that Panahi had received his new sentence in absentia. According to Nili, authorities claim they could not reach Panahi because he was abroad, but the filmmaker has been in Iran since returning home in March and even appeared before a different branch of the Office in September. Nili says Panahi had not been notified of a hearing date for the case.

Panahi’s regular legal punishments from Iranian authorities have long run parallel to his position as one of the country’s most prominent representatives in global cinema. He won the Golden Lion at Venice Film Festival in 2000 for “The Circle,” and the Golden Bear at Berlinale for “Taxi” in 2015.

Panahi often produces his work covertly, incorporating his legal restrictions into his technique and plots. In 2010, the Islamic Revolutionary Court sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and a 20-year ban from filmmaking. In December 2025, he was sentenced to one year in prison on charges of “propaganda activity” against Iran. Panahi was in the U.S. to promote “ It Was Just an Accident ” at the time, leading a campaign that yielded Oscar nominations for Best International Feature Film and Best Original Screenplay.
